title: TB7-12637
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant, PA) and his three children, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (age 18), XXXX XXXX XXXX (age 10), and XXXX XXXX XXXX (age 14) all citizens of Nigeria, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant, PA) and his three children, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (age 18), XXXX XXXX XXXX (age 10), and XXXX XXXX XXXX (age 14) all citizens of Nigeria, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection. They have submitted new evidence in support of their claims and have requested an oral hearing.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD that the Appellants are not Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
The Appellants had their claim for refugee protection heard before the RPD on April 5, 2017 and rejected in a written decision on June 5, 2017.1

The Appellants based their claim on the testimony of the Principal Appellant (PA), a Muslim man who fears his deceased wife's family. The PA alleged before the RPD that his wife was a Christian who died in 2014. After her death, his wife's family wished for him to marry his wife's sister and for the children to attend church. The PA fears his wife's family and, in particular, his brother-in-law who has threatened and assaulted him.

The PA alleges that his brother-in-law wields power with the Nigerian police as well as the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and will use these resources to seek him and his family out throughout Nigeria in order to force him to comply with the family wishes.
The family went into hiding and eventually fled Nigeria and travelled to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2016. They made inland claims for refugee protection on December 29, 2016. THE RPD's FINDINGs

The RPD found that the determinative issue was an internal flight alternative (IFA) for the Appellants in Port Harcourt. It found on a balance of probabilities that the Appellants would be able to move to Port Harcourt and that they would not be found by their agents of persecution. The RPD also found that the Appellants are well educated, speak English, and are resourceful enough that it would not be unreasonable in their circumstances to seek refuge there.

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in its assessment of an IFA. Specifically the Appellants argue that the RPD erred in the following ways: * By not addressing the issue of credibility and yet finding that the Appellants were vague in their description of who they fear and how much power their persecutors wield. * By finding that the police would not seek them out in Port Harcourt, subjecting them to a higher standard of proof than balance of probabilities. * That the RPD was selective in its interpretation of the National Documentation Package (NDP) by finding that there are mechanisms in place to make complaints about police misconduct. * By ignoring evidence of the reach of the XXXX. * By placing minimal emphasis and attention to the second prong of the IFA test. * By ignoring the psychological report of Dr. XXXX on the Principal Appellant.

Subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) provides that Appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claims or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection. It is for the Appellants to make full and detailed submissions in their memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the Appellants.2

In addition, if the new evidence meets one of the explicit legislative factors in subsection 110(4), then the second step of the analysis is for the RAD to apply the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh.3 In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal held that the RAD should assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance and newness. The RAD will apply the Raza factors, minus the "materiality" factor, as this is to be assessed in light of subsection 110(6) only.

For these reasons, the RAD will apply the following factors in considering the Appellant's proposed new evidence. It will first consider whether the evidence passes the test in subsection 110(4). If not, the RAD has no discretion to admit the evidence. If the evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4), the RAD will apply the Raza factors to that evidence.

The Appellants submit a number of news articles on appeal as new evidence. Specifically the Appellant submits ten news articles4 ranging in dates from February 19, 20095 to July 26, 20176. They also submit two news articles after the time limit for appeal, as per Rule 29 of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) rules. Rule 29 application

The Appellants submit two news articles after the perfection of their appeal. These are two articles dated April 16, 2017 and August 11, 2017 respectively and are: * List of the 9 States That Makes Up the Niger Delta Region in Nigeria. Posted April 16, 2017. * N'Delta agitators give northerners, Yoruba quit notice. Published August 11, 2017.7

I have examined both articles and find that the article dated April 16, 2017 does not meet the requirements set out in Rule 29 as it is not relevant, nor is it new evidence; this document lists the 9 states that make up the Niger Delta region and the history of the region, this is covered in the NDP on Nigeria. Furthermore there is no reason it could not have been provided with the Appellants' record.

With respect to the second article, dated August 11, 2017, I find this does meet the Rule 29 factors as the document is relevant to the ethnicity of the Appellants and there was no possibility that the Appellants could have presented the article sooner. This document also meets the requirements in 110(4) as it was published after the RPD decision and therefore was not reasonably available. New evidence on appeal

As part of the Appellants' record they submit a number of new articles. These are; 1. Biafran Pro-Trump rally turns violent in Nigeria. Published January 20, 2017.8 2. High Rate of Rape Incidents in Port Harcourt Suburbs. February 11-17, 2015.9 3. Port Harcourt Ranked Most Dangerous City in the World. February 19, 2009.10 4. See 20 Most Dangerous States You Should Stay Away From in Nigeria-US Government. August 5, 2016.11 5. Yam dealers in Rivers decry police brutality. March 30, 2015.12 6. Explosion Rocks Port Harcourt. July 7, 2017.13 7. Gunmen kidnap 14 passengers in Port Harcourt, demand N14m ransom. July 6, 2017.14 8. Beheading cases portraying Rivers in bad light. July 26, 2017.15 9. Can Lagos Government Severe Ties with NURTW Gangs to Reduce Violence in the City? June 7, 2017.16 10. Two injured as NURTW RTEAN members clash in Ondo. July 26, 2017.17

The Appellants argue that the news articles meet the legislative factors because "we thought we had provided adequate documents to rebut the presumption of Internal Flight Alternative and had not reasonably envisaged that the Panel would not be convinced by [their] testimony."18 I do not agree with this submission. Having reviewed the transcript of the hearing it is clear that the RPD notified the Appellants at the outset of the hearing that internal flight alternative (IFA) will be a determinative issue, among a number of other issues.19 The RPD questioned the Appellants on a number of proposed IFA's including Port Harcourt. I find that the articles that predate the RPD decision in particular, articles number 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, all were reasonably available prior to the RPD decision on June 5, 2017 and therefore do not meet the requirements as set out by section 110(4).

With respect to the other articles, items 6-10, while they are dated after the RPD decision, they do not satisfy the adapted Raza factors for credibility, relevance and newness. The articles refer to violence in Port Harcourt and gang violence in Lagos. While it is the Appellants' contention that this is relevant to their appeal I do not agree. These articles do not refer to any matter that involves the Appellants and only refer to specific incidents of violence covered in the media. For example article 8 refers to the killing of two brothers by beheading and the Rivers police's efforts to arrest the killers. I fail to see the relevance to the Appellants' particular circumstances and find that the articles are not relevant to their appeal. I therefore reject the new evidence. REQUEST FOR A HEARING, ss. 110(6)

The Appellants request a hearing before the RAD. Subsection 110(6) of the IRPA states the following: Hearing (6) The Refugee Appeal Division may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in subsection (3) (a) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal; (b) that is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim; and (c) that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

In this case, the RAD is of the opinion that the document accepted into evidence, N'Delta agitators give northerners, Yoruba quit notice does not justify allowing the refugee protection claim (subsection 110(6) of the IRPA) for reasons that will be explained later in this analysis. Therefore the Appellants' request for a hearing is denied.
In order to find that a claimant has an IFA, the RPD must apply a two-part analysis.20

The RPD correctly stated the two-pronged test and with respect to the first prong asked questions related to the risks the Appellants face in Port Harcourt. The RPD did not make a finding on credibility

The Appellants argue that because the RPD is silent with respect to the credibility of the Appellants, the Appellants' testimony should be considered credible with regard to the sphere of influence of their agents of persecution.

I cannot agree with the Appellants' argument on this point. The PA alleges that his brother-in-law assaulted him and he reported this to the police. He testified before the RPD that the police did not take this report seriously and told him it was a "family matter," and the police told him that his brother-in-law is friends with the "boss." While it is true the RPD made no credibility findings, the RPD did ask the Appellant to explain why it would make a difference that the brother-in-law, their persecutor, is friends with the boss of a police officer they complained to. The PA testified before the RPD that he believes that if he goes anywhere the police will not do anything because of his brother-in-law's influence.

Here the RPD made a sufficiency of evidence finding, and was not obligated to make a credibility finding. The PA was asked if he went to any other division aside from the one police division near his home and he indicated he did not.21 While the PA testified that he believes that his brother-in-law can wield influence over any division, there is simply insufficient evidence for this to be the case, on a balance of probabilities. It is the PA's burden to demonstrate that there is a risk in the IFA and his testimony that he simply believes that his brother-in-law can influence every division is not enough, in my view. I agree here with the analysis of the RPD. Relevance of the National Documentation Package

The PA's evidence is essentially that his brother-in-law had bribed some police officer friends who he has enlisted in his attempts to force the PA to marry his sister-in-law as well as force the children to accept the Christian faith. Having reviewed the entirety of the record I agree with the RPD that there is insufficient evidence to indicate that the police officers who are friends with the brother-in-law are using their connections and influence to search out the Appellants throughout Nigeria.

The Appellants take issue with the RPD findings on the mechanisms of making complaints to the police, indicating that the RPD was selective in relying on the documentation on complaints mechanisms within the police. I do not agree with the Appellants in this regard. The RPD did reference the corruption that is part of the police service as well as the problem of police misconduct.22 The Appellants cite a part of the NDP, the US Department of State Report (DOS) that refers to the lack of effectiveness to examine security force abuses and police misconduct.23 While I agree that there are systemic problems within the security apparatus in Nigeria, the problems refer to police suspects and those that become involved with the police and court system. This case does not involve individuals who are police suspects. The Appellants have not committed any crimes, they are facing a conflict within their extended family. That the brother-in-law of the Principal Appellant is using his influence in the community where the Appellants live, XXXX, does not establish that the police will be used throughout Nigeria to seek out the Appellants when they have not committed any crimes.

While the Appellants contend that the brother-in-law's influence over a few members of the Nigerian police equates with an interest and ability for the Nigerian police to track down the Appellants all over Nigeria, I do not find this is borne out by the evidence submitted.

There is simply no evidence to suggest that this matter is extending beyond the scope and influence of the in-laws. That the brother-in-law is able to influence his friends who are police is not enough to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the police will be seeking them out throughout Nigeria to force the Appellants to worship in the Christian faith or for the PA to marry his deceased wife's sister.
The Appellants' characterization that it is the Nigeria police who are the agents of persecution is misstated and mischaracterized, in my view. The influence of the XXXX

The Appellants also refer to the fact that the brother-in-law is a member of the XXXX and would use his influence to track them down through the union.24 The evidence before the RPD was that the XXXX is a XXXX XXXX that is often engaged in illegal activities, such as the collection of illegal tolls.25 The Appellants submit that the RPD ignored their testimony that the brother-in-law has vowed to search for them everywhere and that the XXXX is located in every state. Again, I cannot agree with the submissions by the Appellant that the RPD erred.

The Appellants assert that the brother-in-law is highly motivated to locate them and because he runs a XXXX business he would be able to locate them in Port Harcourt. The RPD rejected the PA's evidence on this point based on insufficiency of evidence. I find the RPD was correct, the Appellants have not shown, on a balance of probabilities, that the brother-in-law would be able to locate them in Port Harcourt. The PA's testimony equates ownership of a transport XXXX with an ability to track them down. There was no evidence to indicate whether the brother-in-law's business even XXXX to Port Harcourt. The testimony on record is that he has XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.26 Neither this fact nor the fact that he is a member of the XXXX is sufficient evidence to suggest that they could gather intelligence on the whereabouts of the Appellants in Port Harcourt. The Reasonableness argument

The Appellants submit that the RPD failed to properly evaluate the second prong of the IFA test. In reviewing the RPD's decision the RPD examined the language of the Appellants, the education of the PA, and refers to the Appellants' ability to settle in Canada. I agree with the Appellants that this comparison to Canada is not a correct examination of the how reasonable it is to expect the Appellants to settle in Port Harcourt. Ethnicity and its impacts upon employment

The Appellants submit that the PA would be unable to find work in Port Harcourt due to the discrimination non-indigenes face in accessing public sector jobs. They cite the Response to Information Request from 201227 that refers to the difficulties faced by non-indigenes of the state to access public sector jobs. While the Appellants cite the evidence that indicates that public sector work is for those from Rivers State, and that in Port Harcourt there may be difficulty in accessing jobs in the region's oil industry as the jobs may more often go to indigenes of the Niger Delta region, the same document indicates that in other industries such as the private sector, hiring is based upon merit.28

The RAD did consider this evidence in relation to the PA's particular profile. He was self-employed in Nigeria running his own business.29 The PA has 7 years of college and a history of self-employment and trading.30 While indigene status is relevant in Port Harcourt there is evidence that there are opportunities for others.31 The RAD finds that the PA's profile is such that, on a balance of probabilities, he would be able to find work in certain sectors should he and his family go to Port Harcourt.

While the Appellants also refer to the cost of living in Port Harcourt32 as a detriment to living there the RAD finds that the PA's personal profile of having employment experience and some education places him in a good position to find work and support himself and his family.

More generally, the Appellants raised the issue of indigene status in relocating to Port Harcourt and refers to their Yoruba ethnicity as one that is not indigenous to the area. The evidence specifically uses the terms indigene (or insider) when describing inhabitants from an ethnic group native to an area and "settler" (or outsider) when the inhabitant is from a minority ethnic group not indigenous to the area.33 The Appellants argue that their ethnic group is not native to the area of Port Harcourt and therefore it would not be reasonable to live there as they would suffer discrimination.

The evidence does certainly address discrimination that many non-indigenes face when attempting to relocate within Nigeria and there are systemic and legislative problems that limit individuals from moving and settling freely throughout Nigeria. Part of the challenge however is in how the term indigene is defined- for example in Ogun state it is tied to both ethnic group and land ownership.34 Furthermore while the term indigene is referred to in the Nigerian Constitution it is not defined. The evidence seems to indicate that conferring indigene status can be arbitrary as there are ethnic groups who have lived in one area for generations but may not be historically associated with the area. Indigene status is used in many cases in Nigeria to exclude outsiders from access to land, education, employment etc. While it is an important distinction to understand in the context of relocating within Nigeria, the same document does distinguish between settling in large urban centres versus smaller areas. "...Indigeneship status is less important in big cities such as Lagos, Abuja, and Port Harcourt than it is in other places, in terms of access to public jobs or ownership of land, because the indigene population in these areas has been 'overwhelmed' by migrants to the cities."35

The Appellants are ethnically Yoruba, speak Yoruba and English as indicated on their Basis of Claim (BOC)36 and are of the Muslim faith. Port Harcourt is a large city of over 2.3 million people and is located a substantial distance from Abeokuta. The evidence also indicates that English is the language used for "most governmental administrative functions, education, business, and mass media". 37 Given that the IFA is to another large city that is cited in the documentary evidence as having fewer problems with respect to the indigene issue, the RAD finds that the indigeneship status of the Appellants does not preclude them from living and working in Port Harcourt.

Furthermore given the objective evidence of the use of English as the language used in education, the minor Appellants' command of the language means they would more easily be able to integrate into the education system in Port Harcourt. Conflict in the Niger Delta

The Appellants also refer to the ongoing conflict in the Niger Delta related to the oil industry as further evidence that Port Harcourt is unviable as an IFA.38 I find that this specific piece of objective evidence,39 relied upon by the Appellants, does not support their argument that the objective evidence demonstrates that an IFA to Port Harcourt is unreasonable. The evidence refers to protests over environmental damage, kidnappings for ransom, kidnapping of oil workers, and attacks on oil facilities as evidence of the problems in the region. The fears expressed by the Appellants are based upon the general state of conflict and criminal activity in the region and this does not pose a risk to the Appellants based upon their profile, on a balance of probabilities. Article on the Yoruba

The Appellants submitted a news article published on August 11, 2017 that refers to a group that call themselves the Coalition of Niger Delta Agitators who have called for northerners and the Yoruba to leave the Niger Delta region by October 1, 2017. They are referred to as having made attacks on oil installations in the region.40

I have reviewed this article and find that while there is evidence of discrimination against the Yoruba by a specific group, this article does not demonstrate that this is sanctioned by the government or that the demands of this group have been met. There is no evidence before me to indicate that these unrealistic demands were met and that Yoruba who live in the Niger Delta region have all been driven out.

I find that while the article does speak to the ongoing tension in the area it is not persuasive to suggest that the Appellants' ethnicity is going to hinder them from settling in Port Harcourt, on a balance of probabilities. Psychological state of the PA

The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to consider the psychological evaluation conducted by Dr. XXXX in its analysis of an IFA. The RPD did refer to the psychological evaluation in its reasons but I agree that the RPD did not demonstrate how it considered the evaluation. I have read the evaluation41 and find that while it does refer to the PA suffering from XXXX and symptoms of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the report contains no assessment of the mental health impact of the PA and his children relocating anywhere in Nigeria to avoid his in-laws. For these reasons I find that the psychological evaluation and the state of the PA is not sufficient evidence to find that he and his children cannot relocate to Port Harcourt on a balance of probabilities.

While it is possible that the Appellants may face some hardships in relocating to Port Harcourt based upon the economic situation and discrimination, I find that these challenges are the same for many people living in Port Harcourt. I find that these challenges do not meet the threshold required to make the proposed IFA unreasonable. Therefore it is not unreasonable for the Appellants in this situation to relocate to another part of Nigeria, far away from their in-laws and their sphere of influence, rather than seek international refugee protection. For these reasons the appeal is dismissed.

Having considered the entire record, I find that I agree with the conclusion made by the RPD that the Appellants have a viable IFA in Port Harcourt. As a result there is no serious possibility that the Appellants would be persecuted, or would be personally subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture or to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Port Harcourt. They have also not provided sufficient evidence that relocating to Port Harcourt is unreasonable in their circumstances.

The RPD decision is confirmed and the appeal is dismissed.
